questions.q: A 35-year-old farmer presents with a chronic ulcer on his forearm with raised, violaceous borders and satellite nodules along the lymphatics. KOH preparation shows thick-walled, brown, muriform cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Chromoblastomycosis presents with warty, cauliflower-like plaques and the pathognomonic 'copper pennies' (muriform/sclerotic bodies) on KOH/histology. These are brown, thick-walled, septate cells dividing by septation.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman develops a malar rash, oral ulcers, and joint pain. Skin biopsy shows vacuolar interface dermatitis with thickening of the basement membrane. Which immunofluorescence pattern is most characteristic?
opts: Granular IgG + C3 at the DEJ (lupus band test)
questions.exp: Lupus erythematosus shows granular deposition of IgG, IgM, IgA, and complement (C3) at the dermo-epidermal junction on direct immunofluorescence — the 'lupus band test'. This is positive even in uninvolved skin in systemic LE.

questions.q: A 22-year-old man presents with grouped tense vesicles on an erythematous base over the trunk and extremities. Direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgA deposition at the dermo-epidermal junction. The most appropriate first-line treatment is:
questions.exp: Linear IgA disease is treated with Dapsone as first-line therapy. The classic DIF shows linear IgA at the DEJ. Dapsone is also first-line for dermatitis herpetiformis.

questions.q: A 45-year-old man presents with a painless, indurated ulcer on the glans penis. Dark-field microscopy reveals motile spirochetes. Which of the following best describes the causative organism?
questions.exp: Treponema pallidum, the cause of primary syphilis, is a motile spirochete with tight regular coils that cannot be cultured in vitro. It is identified by dark-field microscopy from the chancre.

questions.q: A 6-year-old child presents with honey-colored crusted lesions around the nose and mouth that developed after a minor abrasion. The most likely causative organism is:
questions.exp: Impetigo in children is most commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus (bullous impetigo) or a mixed infection. S. aureus is now the predominant cause of non-bullous (crusted) impetigo, with honey-colored crusts being characteristic.

questions.q: A leprosy patient on multidrug therapy develops sudden fever, erythematous tender nodules over the skin, iritis, and painful nerve swelling. Slit-skin smear shows many bacilli. Which reaction type is this and what is the treatment?
questions.exp: Erythema Nodosum Leprosum (ENL / Type 2 reaction) occurs in lepromatous and borderline lepromatous leprosy. It is an immune complex–mediated reaction treated with thalidomide (drug of choice) or steroids. MDT is continued.

questions.q: A 55-year-old man presents with a pearly, translucent nodule with telangiectasias on the nose that occasionally bleeds. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Nodular basal cell carcinoma classically presents as a pearly papule or nodule with rolled borders and telangiectasias, most commonly on the face (nose, periorbital). It is the most common skin cancer.

questions.q: A 30-year-old HIV-positive patient presents with soft, skin-colored papules with central umbilication all over the face. The CD4 count is 90 cells/µL. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Molluscum contagiosum caused by Molluscipoxvirus presents with umbilicated, flesh-colored papules. In immunocompromised patients (low CD4), lesions are numerous, large ('giant molluscum'), and facial, mimicking other infections like cryptococcosis.

questions.q: During a Mohs micrographic surgery, which of the following is the key advantage over standard wide local excision for basal cell carcinoma?
opts: Ability to perform under general anesthesia
Complete en face margin examination with tissue mapping
questions.exp: Mohs surgery examines 100% of peripheral and deep margins (en face/horizontal sections) in real-time while sparing maximum normal tissue. Standard excision examines only <1% of margins (bread-loaf sections).

questions.q: A patient on long-term dapsone therapy for dermatitis herpetiformis develops hemolytic anemia and methemoglobinemia. Which enzyme deficiency predisposes to severe dapsone toxicity?
questions.exp: G6PD (Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase) deficiency markedly increases sensitivity to dapsone-induced oxidative hemolysis. G6PD screening is recommended before starting dapsone. Methemoglobinemia is also a dose-dependent side effect.

questions.q: A 40-year-old presents with extensive flaccid bullae and erosions predominantly involving the trunk and mucous membranes. Histology shows suprabasal acantholysis. Which autoantibody is pathognomonic?
questions.exp: Pemphigus vulgaris involves anti-Dsg3 antibodies (mucous membrane involvement) with or without anti-Dsg1 (skin involvement). Suprabasal acantholysis (tombstone cells) on histology and intercellular IgG on DIF are characteristic.

questions.q: A 25-year-old presents with painless ulcer-like lesions with a 'soap bubble' appearance on X-ray of the tibia and a positive Donovan bodies finding on tissue smear. The diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Donovanosis (Granuloma inguinale) is caused by Klebsiella granulomatis. It presents with painless, beefy-red, progressive ulcers. Donovan bodies (bipolar-staining intracellular organisms in macrophages) on Giemsa/Wright stain confirm the diagnosis.

questions.q: A newborn presents with generalized skin peeling within 24 hours of birth. The skin separates at the level of the granular layer. A mutation in which gene is most likely responsible?
questions.exp: Netherton syndrome is caused by SPINK5 mutations (encoding LEKTI, a serine protease inhibitor). It presents with ichthyosis linearis circumflexa, trichorrhexis invaginata (bamboo hair), and atopic manifestations. Peeling is due to unchecked serine protease activity in the stratum corneum.

questions.q: Which clinical finding best differentiates borderline tuberculoid (BT) from borderline lepromatous (BL) leprosy on skin examination?
opts: Loss of sensation in the lesion
questions.exp: Skin smear is negative in BT leprosy (paucibacillary) but positive in BL leprosy (multibacillary). BT lesions are few, well-defined with clear centers; BL lesions are numerous, less well-defined. Both can have nerve involvement.

questions.q: A 50-year-old woman on hydroxyurea for polycythemia vera develops painful leg ulcers, hyperpigmented macules, and longitudinal melanonychia. The mechanism of this drug's toxicity on skin is:
opts: Inhibition of ribonucleotide reductase causing keratinocyte toxicity
questions.exp: Hydroxyurea inhibits ribonucleotide reductase, impairing DNA synthesis. Long-term use causes leg ulcers (especially over pressure points), hyperpigmentation, dermatomyositis-like eruption, and melanonychia. It is a well-recognized side effect of chronic use.

questions.q: A 32-year-old presents with well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scales on the elbows and scalp. The Auspitz sign is positive. Histopathology would most likely show:
questions.exp: Psoriasis histopathology shows regular epidermal acanthosis, parakeratosis, elongated rete ridges, dilated tortuous capillaries in dermal papillae, and Munro's microabscesses (neutrophils in parakeratotic stratum corneum).

questions.q: A 20-year-old student presents with annular, scaly plaques with central clearing on the groin. KOH shows septate hyphae. He is prescribed oral terbinafine. Terbinafine's mechanism of action is:
opts: Disruption of cell membrane by binding ergosterol
questions.exp: Terbinafine inhibits squalene epoxidase, causing accumulation of toxic squalene within the fungal cell. Azoles inhibit CYP51 (lanosterol demethylase). Echinocandins inhibit β-1,3-glucan synthase. Polyenes (amphotericin) bind ergosterol.

questions.q: A 15-year-old boy presents with large, flaccid bullae on the extremities, mucous membrane involvement, and target lesions following herpes simplex infection. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Erythema multiforme major (distinct from SJS) presents with typical/atypical target lesions, mucous membrane involvement, and is strongly associated with HSV infection. SJS is drug-induced with >10% BSA epidermal detachment, while EM major involves <10% detachment.

questions.q: A 60-year-old woman presents with sclerotic plaques on the trunk that are ivory-white with a violaceous border. The plaques are indurated and cannot be pinched. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Morphea (localized scleroderma) presents with sclerotic plaques with ivory centers and a lilac/violaceous border (lilac ring), representing active inflammation. Unlike systemic sclerosis, there is no Raynaud's phenomenon, sclerodactyly, or internal organ involvement.

questions.q: A patient presents with multiple milia, comedones, and hyperpigmented scars on the face. She reports using a potent fluorinated topical steroid on her face for 6 months. Which complication is she least likely to have?
questions.exp: Long-term topical steroid use on the face causes steroid rosacea, perioral dermatitis, skin atrophy, telangiectasia, striae, and tinea incognito (masked fungal infection). Acanthosis nigricans is associated with insulin resistance and systemic conditions, not topical steroids.

questions.q: A 4-year-old child presents with clustered vesicles on an erythematous base at the vermilion border of the lip recurring every 2 months. Tzanck smear shows multinucleated giant cells. The virus responsible belongs to:
questions.exp: Recurrent herpes labialis is caused by HSV-1, belonging to the Herpesviridae family. Tzanck smear showing multinucleated giant cells (with nuclear molding) is characteristic of herpesvirus infections (HSV-1, HSV-2, VZV).

questions.q: During patch testing, a patient's test site shows erythema, induration, and vesicles at 48 and 96 hours to a specific allergen. This reaction is mediated primarily by:
opts: CD4+ T lymphocyte–mediated type IV hypersensitivity
questions.exp: Allergic contact dermatitis (ACD) tested by patch testing is a type IV (delayed-type) hypersensitivity reaction mediated by CD4+ Th1 and CD8+ T cells. The reaction peaks at 48–96 hours, distinguishing it from irritant contact dermatitis.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with diffuse hyperpigmentation affecting sun-exposed areas, mucous membranes, and palmar creases. Biopsy shows melanin in both keratinocytes and melanophages. Which investigation is most important next?
questions.exp: Generalized hyperpigmentation involving mucous membranes and palmar creases is classic for Addison's disease (primary adrenal insufficiency) due to excess ACTH stimulating melanocytes. The ACTH (cosyntropin) stimulation test is the gold standard for diagnosis.

questions.q: A 35-year-old man with chronic plaque psoriasis fails methotrexate. He is started on adalimumab. Before initiating adalimumab, which mandatory screening is required?
opts: VDRL and hepatitis B surface antigen
Tuberculin skin test (TST) or IGRA, hepatitis B, and CXR
questions.exp: Before starting TNF-α inhibitors (adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab), mandatory screening includes latent TB (TST or IGRA + CXR), hepatitis B (HBsAg, anti-HBc), and CBC. TB can reactivate with anti-TNF therapy.

questions.q: A 70-year-old farmer presents with a slow-growing, flesh-colored tumor on the ear with a central keratin-filled crater that appeared over 6 weeks and is now involuting spontaneously. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Keratoacanthoma is a rapidly growing, self-involuting, crater-shaped tumor with a central keratin plug on sun-exposed skin of elderly men. Despite its benign behavior, it is histologically similar to SCC; many treat it as well-differentiated SCC.

questions.q: A child presents with soft, nontender, flesh-colored papules with central umbilication on the eyelids and face. These have appeared in the setting of a chronic pruritic rash with lichenification in the antecubital fossae. The underlying predisposing condition is most likely:
questions.exp: Atopic dermatitis (eczema) causes impaired skin barrier function and immune dysregulation (Th2 skewing), predisposing to molluscum contagiosum (MCV) spreading in the setting of eczema. This is known as eczema molluscatum.

questions.q: A 28-year-old HIV-positive man develops discrete, non-pruritic, hyper- and hypopigmented macules on the trunk and back. Wood's lamp shows no fluorescence. Skin scrapings with KOH show 'spaghetti and meatballs' pattern. Treatment of choice is:
questions.exp: Tinea versicolor (Pityriasis versicolor) shows the 'spaghetti and meatballs' pattern on KOH (short hyphae + rounded yeast forms of Malassezia). Single-dose itraconazole 400 mg or 200 mg daily × 7 days is effective oral therapy. Terbinafine is less effective for Malassezia.

questions.q: A 55-year-old presents with firm, non-pitting leg edema, woody induration, and hyperpigmentation. He has a history of recurrent cellulitis. The overlying skin cannot be lifted from the underlying tissue. This clinical sign is called:
questions.exp: Kaposi-Stemmer sign (inability to pinch/lift skin at the base of the second toe or dorsum of foot/leg) is pathognomonic for lymphedema. Woody non-pitting edema with recurrent cellulitis describes chronic lymphedema.

questions.q: A melanoma excised from the back measures 1.8 mm in Breslow thickness, with ulceration and no satellite lesions. According to AJCC 8th edition staging, the T stage is:
questions.exp: AJCC 8th edition: T2 = 1.01–2.0 mm Breslow thickness. Suffix 'a' = without ulceration; 'b' = with ulceration. Therefore 1.8 mm with ulceration = T2b. T3 = 2.01–4.0 mm.

questions.q: A 3-year-old child develops multiple fluid-filled vesicles in crops over the trunk and face, with lesions in various stages of evolution. A schoolmate had a similar illness 2 weeks ago. The virus responsible is also associated with which dermatological complication in elderly immunocompromised patients?
questions.exp: Varicella-zoster virus (VZV) causes chickenpox (primary infection) and later reactivates as herpes zoster (shingles) in elderly/immunocompromised patients. Zoster presents as painful dermatomal vesicular eruption.

questions.q: A patient with longstanding vitiligo affecting >50% of body surface area wants to achieve cosmetic uniformity. The most appropriate management strategy is:
opts: NB-UVB phototherapy to re-pigment remaining areas
Chemical depigmentation with monobenzyl ether of hydroquinone (MBEH)
Topical tacrolimus 0.1% to all affected areas
Punch grafting of all affected areas
questions.exp: When >50% BSA is affected with stable vitiligo and re-pigmentation is not feasible, depigmentation of the remaining normally pigmented skin with MBEH (Benoquin) achieves cosmetic uniformity. This is a permanent and irreversible procedure.
